newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS - Kazakh oil sell-off fogged by uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kazakh oil sell-off fogged by uncertainty.

text.p: Kazakhstan's multi-billion dollar oil privatisation programme gathered pace on Monday with the sale of its Atyrau oil refinery, but investors in the former Soviet republic say the sell-off remains fogged by uncertainty.

Essex Refinery Corp, registered in the British Virgin Islands, won a tender for a 53.1 percent stake in the Atyrau refinery, a senior official with Kazakhstan's State Privatisation Committee told Reuters.
Under the deal, Essex will invest over $1 billion in the refinery, which has an annual capacity of 4.5 million tonnes.
The official said a tender for the republic's largest oil concern, Mangistaumunaigaz, is set to close at the end of this week.
In scale, the sell-off is unprecedented for a former Soviet republic.
The government, desperate to pay off an increasingly unpopular backlog of unpaid pensions and wages, is looking to cash in on its oil assets as fast as it can.

But despite billions of barrels of crude lying beneath the battered, ailing enterprises strewn across the desert and steppe in a country five times the size of France, western oil majors have been reluctant to take the plunge.
It is the little-known juniors trying to boost humble stocks or obscure offshore companies like Essex Refinery Corp which are doing the running.
Only last week, Calgary-based junior Triton-Vuko Energy Group Ltd won a 94.5 percent stake in Kazakhstan's sickly Karazhanbasmunai oil enterprise in the republic's western Mangistau region.
While production has slumped since Kazakh independence in 1991, the concern still sits on reserves of 85 million tonnes of crude and another 225 million tonnes in estimated reserves.
Typically, the Kazakh government has given no details of the deal.
"The smaller companies are more suited to Kazakhstan right now," said a western analyst based in the Kazakh capital Almaty, who declined to be named.

He said executives with major western oil companies were put off by the lack of transparency and what many in the tight-lipped business say privately is deep-rooted corruption in Kazakh privatisation.

The low number of export pipelines from the landlocked country, all of which run through neighbouring Russia which keeps a jealous eye on its former colony's oil riches, are a concern for the risk-conscious majors.
The enterprises' entrenched Soviet-era bosses have also proved unattractive to oil majors, concerned that they could get in the way of any major overhaul needed to make them profitable.
"They are good engineers but no good at finance," said one senior Kazakh reform official concerned at the delay in privatisation by the enterprise's directors.

However, the western majors appear to be waking up, with Amoco Corp last week, taking a stake in a pipeline project and underlining its interest in the huge Uzen oil field, with estimated oil reserves of 150 million tonnes.
